This drives the service status. Change the
prose here, then run `python3 docs/publish_service_status.py` to refresh the group's shared
sheet from it.

Refactoring onto the library template means every service is built the same way, in two files.

One file holds the maths and never opens or saves anything. The second file does the opening and saving. It reads the input data,
calls the maths, and writes the results.

Every service joins its results to the same country list and builds its results
page the same way.

The fields mean: **category** is what the code does to produce the number, on a scale from
reading a published value to running a model here. **method** is how the number is computed.
**ours** is whether we can compute the number ourselves, or only read someone else's. **code** is
the engineering work we did. **number** is what the figure is and what it was checked against.
**need** is what we are waiting on from someone else. **signed off** is whether the service meets
the thirteen conditions below.

**What signed off means.**

The standard the account is built to: **somebody who wants to reproduce a GEP number should be able
to read this repository and follow every step, without opening anyone else's.** They will need the
data — base_data holds inputs from many authors and always will — but not another codebase, and not
a person to explain the missing part.

That is what `signed off: green` asserts. Thirteen conditions, each of which has already failed
somewhere and been caught:

1. **Our code produces the number.** Not the author's code run by us. A service whose only working
   pipeline is the author's own repository has not been ported, however faithful the output.
2. **The repository is self-sufficient.** Every step from input to published figure is in this
   library. An author's raster staged in base_data is an input like any other and is fine; a
   procedure that says "clone their repo and run six commands" is not part of the pipeline and
   cannot be a step in it.
3. **The published outputs come from the current code.** Regenerated after the last change that
   moves a number, not carried over from a run whose code no longer exists. `skip_existing` makes
   this failure silent, so it has to be checked rather than assumed.
4. **The grid and the cell area are stated** (H12), because that is where a density becomes a total.
5. **What the reproduction cannot test is stated.** Matching an author's output tests our port; it
   cannot see an error their code also makes. Where the reference shares our lineage, say so.
6. **The three gates pass** — harmonization, consistency, deck.
7. **No open question blocks the number.** A question for the account to decide is not a blocker; a
   question whose answer would change the figure is.
8. **The service is the agreed set of files, and no more.** Four:
   `<service>_functions.py` (the maths, opens nothing), `<service>_tasks.py` (the IO),
   `<service>_initialize.py` (the task trees), `run_<service>.py` (a thin runner), plus
   `test_<service>.py` and any `run_<service>_shock.py`. A service that carries its own `_utils.py`
   or a `scripts/` directory has a private copy of something that belongs in the shared utilities,
   in hazelbean, or in its own two files — and a private copy drifts. Flood's `scripts/` was not
   committed at all until 2026-08-29, so the repository could not produce a flood number.
9. **No unanswered question with the author.** A thread we have opened and they have not closed
   leaves the service provisional, even when our own number would not move. If we have written to
   them saying we think something in their pipeline is wrong, we are waiting on the answer, and a
   sign-off before it arrives claims a settlement we do not have. An unsent draft counts as open:
   the question exists whether or not we have got round to asking it. Closed means answered, or
   deliberately not asked and the entry says why.

10. **A cold start has been run, and the run is named.** Not inferred from the paths resolving: a
   fresh project directory, nothing reused, reading data a second person can reach. Every other
   condition passed for pollination on a machine where its inputs existed nowhere else and its
   yield and production tasks finished in under a second by reusing outputs nobody had rebuilt --
   0.64 seconds for 158 crop rasters, which is the tell. Twenty of its twenty input references
   were absent from the shared base_data while the entry said the repository was self-sufficient.
   The standard this list serves is that somebody who clones the repository and has base_data gets
   the number, so the only evidence that counts is having done exactly that. Record which project
   directory the run used, when, and the figure it returned, because a cold start nobody can point
   to is a claim rather than a check.

11. **The service is on the account's shared conventions, not merely explicit about its own.**
   Condition 4 asks that the grid and cell area be *stated*; this asks that they be *the house
   ones*. Pollination ran on a 6371 km sphere for months, stated correctly the whole time, and
   condition 4 passed it every day -- a number can be fully explained and still not comparable
   with the number beside it. The conventions, which are the authors' own consistency list of
   2026-08-31:

   - **The country list is r250**, one row per country, and split countries summed once.
   - **The base year is 2019 and the dollars are 2019 dollars.** FAOSTAT reports current-year
     dollars, so a service reading it at 2019 needs no conversion and a service reading another
     year does. Pollination's price window sat centred on 2020 for a 2019 account until
     2026-08-30, with a deflator existing only to cross the gap it should not have had.
   - **The grid is WGS84 and the cell area comes from hazelbean's `ha_per_cell` pyramid**, so
     every service measures a cell the same way. Not a sphere, not a constant, not a per-tile
     midpoint latitude -- each of those has been found here, and each moved a total.
   - **A true zero is 0 and missing data is NA**, and the entry says which a country got and why.
     Coastal protection for a landlocked country is a zero; a country the model could not reach is
     not.
   - **Shared parameters are the shared values**: the discount rate, the value of a statistical
     life, the CWoN rental rates. Landslides uses OECD VSL while air filtration uses a
     GDP-adjusted US-anchored one, which is two answers to one question inside one account.

   Stating a departure is not meeting the condition. A service that departs deliberately says so
   and stays amber until the account agrees the departure, because the point of the convention is
   that figures can be added together.

12. **A reproduction is checked, not claimed.** Where an entry says our figure reproduces someone
   else's, three things have to be true and each has failed here. The reference output is staged in
   base_data, so a second person can look at it: crop production carried "reproduces the reference
   table" for weeks while the same entry recorded that the reference was in nobody's repository. A
   test compares against it, so the agreement survives the next change rather than resting on
   somebody having checked once. And the comparison is made against the **cold start**, not a warm
   directory, and against **every** run present rather than one named path -- when that test was
   first written to scan every run it immediately failed on two superseded cold starts from earlier
   the same day, either of which would otherwise have stood as evidence for code that no longer
   existed. A reproduction nobody can re-run is the same kind of claim condition 10 rules out.

13. **The author's repository could be deleted tomorrow.** Not merely that our code runs it
   (condition 1) or that every step is in this library (condition 2), but that nothing in the
   pipeline *or its verification* reaches into somebody's checkout: their inputs staged in
   base_data, their reference outputs staged beside them, and no path in `es_parameters` leaving
   base_data at all, which H22 checks. A reference path into a checkout is indistinguishable from
   one into base_data right until the checkout is gone, and then the failure lands on whoever
   cloned the repo next rather than on us -- erosion carried 39 absolute paths into an author's
   MSI workspace for exactly this reason.

   And the second half: where our code departs from theirs it departs because ours is better, and
   the entry says why. Reproducing somebody is the evidence that we understood their pipeline; it
   is not the goal. Crop subsistence reproduces theirs exactly and then publishes a different
   number, because their units disagree with their own sources and their extrapolation fits the
   own-consumption level on the largest term in the formula that produced it. Publishing their
   arithmetic once we knew that would have been repeating a mistake with our name on it.

Green means all thirteen. **amber** means the number is usable and at least one condition is open, with
the entry saying which. **red** means the number should not be quoted yet.

⚠⚠ **A fidelity-only check no longer passes.** This used to read that a service could be green
while its only check was that it reproduced the author's output, provided condition 5 said so. That
exemption let green mean "our engineering is complete and legible" while the number rested entirely
on somebody else's data and somebody else's method, which is not what a reader takes green to mean.
Nine services reproduce their source **because they share its lineage** -- terrestrial carbon, both
fisheries rows, crop, water quality, air filtration, storm mitigation, hydropower and water use --
and that agreement cannot see an error the original also makes. Pollination is the sharpest case:
the dependence table, the FAOSTAT bulks, the CropGrids and Monfreda grids are all the author's, so
reproducing his pair to the cent tests our port and nothing else.

Condition 5 therefore now requires more than saying so. Either the check is independent of the
source's lineage, or the entry names what an independent check would have to be and green waits for
it. Green is a claim that the number is ours and that somebody could find it wrong; a port nobody
can contradict is amber however clean the code.

The five categories, in ascending order of what the code does.

**1. Reads a published value — 1 account.** The per-country figure already exists in a file. We
open it and reshape it to the house table, and no valuation happens. *Urban cooling* is the one:
the city-month valuations are ours, but the reported figure is parsed from a dollar column in a
committed file.

**2. Rescales a published rate — 2 accounts.** Someone published a rate rather than a value, and
one or two operations turn it into dollars. *Mining production* is a rent share times GDP times
0.49; *extractive energy* is the sum of three published per-fuel rent columns. Real arithmetic,
but the economics is entirely theirs.

**3. Table arithmetic — 12 accounts.** A quantity, a price and an attribution multiplied over
tables, with no grids involved. This is the bulk of the library: crop production, livestock, both
fisheries rows, energy production, hydropower, water use, air filtration, sandstorm prevention,
wildfires, water quality and coastal protection.

**4. Raster arithmetic — 7 accounts.** The value cannot be reached without processing grids, cell
by cell, multiplied and summed into countries. *Pollination* multiplies 158 production grids by
price and by each crop's pollinator dependence per cell; *terrestrial carbon* builds density
rasters. Also coastal carbon, ntfp, timber, floods and stormwater.

**5. Process model run here — 3 accounts.** A model with dynamics of its own runs inside the
pipeline. *Erosion* runs InVEST SDR with sediment routing, *landslides* computes slope stability
twice for every pixel, and *recreation* runs a gravity model allocating visits into scored sites.

`category` and `ours` answer different questions. A service can run a model here and still not be
ours, because the coefficients or the physical quantity come from elsewhere. Wildfires is the
clearest case: the valuation runs here, and the regression coefficients underneath it do not.

**The ladder measures work, not confidence.** Read as a quality ranking it gets things backwards.
The account without a usable number sits at the top of it: stormwater reports retained volume and
no dollar total because its price is a placeholder of 1. Crop production, down at table
arithmetic, reproduces its reference table exactly.

**One label per service hides a split.** Several services compute part of the value and read the
rest, and the category can only name the heaviest thing the code does. Water quality computes its
dollar figure and reads the international-dollar one it reports; coastal protection computes the
mangrove half and reads the coral half; ntfp computes the accessible area and reads the value per
hectare. `ours` is where that lives.


## Terrestrial Carbon

- **subgroup:** terrestrial
- **module:** terrestrial_carbon
- **category:** raster arithmetic
- **in the library:** yes
- **run:** yes
- **ours:** yes
- **method:** Carbon density by climate zone and land-cover class, times hectares per cell, summed to countries, times the rental social cost of carbon. Rental is not the full social cost: the full cost is what a tonne is worth as an asset, and the rental is one year's service from holding it. The account is an annual flow, so it takes the yearly service. The rental is P(1 - e^-r), which at 2 percent turns an asset worth $665.87 a tonne of carbon into $13.19 a year. The quantity is a carbon density raster built here from a zone-by-class density table and the land-cover map.
- **total:** $5.365T
- **code:** Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Corrected division by the wrong baseline for the shock, and corrected a double-count that had entered split countries once per sub-region.
- **grid:** WGS84 geographic on the shared 10 arc-second pyramid. Cell area is the per-latitude `ha_per_cell` raster, multiplied into the density in terrestrial_carbon_tasks.py:146. Correct: a geographic grid needs a per-cell area and this carries one.
- **reference:** The manuscript total. NOT independent of us in the part that matters, since we reproduce a figure computed from the same density table and land-cover map. The double-count we fixed was ours to find, which is what an agreement of this kind cannot surface.
- **replicated:** Yes, the manuscript total. ⚠ Same lineage, so it tests our port rather than the science.
- **decided:** -
- **number:** Values the carbon stored in land ecosystems, priced at the rental social cost of carbon. Reproduces the manuscript total of $5.365T, after fixing a double-count that entered split countries once per sub-region (China six times, 23.5 percent overstatement). Priced at the rental social cost of carbon at 2 percent. The 3 percent sensitivity is a run of its own and gives $3.4627T. There is no 1 percent column. 
- **need:** Two decisions on the discount rate. First, whether carbon prices are taken to grow. The r in the rental formula is the net rate, the discount rate minus the growth rate of carbon prices, so our 2 percent column assumes prices do not grow. The table already carries the alternative: a column at 3 percent discounting minus 2.2 percent growth, so 0.8 percent net, which gives $2.29 a tonne against our $13.19. Second, the 1 percent price. It cannot be derived from carbon_prices.xlsx, which holds only $181.60 per tonne of CO2 at 2 percent and $78.53 at 3 percent. Not clear where they came from. 

- **signed off:** amber: examined, and at least one of the twelve conditions is not yet verified. ⚠ **10 is unmet here and everywhere**: no service in this library has been built from an empty project directory, so every claim that a clone reproduces it rests on the input paths resolving rather than on a run. ⚠ **11 is unverified**: the base year is 2019 across every service, but the country list, the true-zero-against-missing rule and the shared parameters have not been checked service by service
## Coastal Carbon

- **subgroup:** coastal
- **module:** coastal_carbon
- **category:** raster arithmetic
- **in the library:** yes
- **run:** yes
- **ours:** yes
- **method:** Mapped mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass area, times carbon density per habitat and pool, priced like terrestrial carbon. The quantity is habitat area measured here from the mapped mangrove, salt marsh and seagrass extents.
- **total:** $17.72bn seaward only. $58.75bn both sides.
- **code:** Merged the author's rework, then refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Checked the refactored code against the original on identical inputs.
- **grid:** WGS84 geographic on the shared pyramid, cell area from `ha_per_cell`. ⚠ The grid was never the problem here. Its extent was: a 0/1 mask credited a habitat with every cell it touched, putting mangrove at 29.08 Mha against 14.69 Mha of polygon and salt marsh near three times its area. Mangrove and salt marsh now weight each cell by the share the habitat covers. ⚠ Seagrass does NOT, because its density is a polygon attribute, so it still sums polygon areas that overlap.
- **reference:** The author's reported numbers. ⚠ That agreement held while the extent was roughly doubled, so it never tested the extent. The coverage fix moves mangrove -48.8 percent and salt marsh -66.1 percent, and the EEZ-only total from $22.84bn to $17.72bn. Yanxu has not yet been told.
- **replicated:** Yes, until we fixed the extent. The fix moves the EEZ-only total -22.4 percent, so we now differ from the author deliberately, and he has not been told.
- **decided:** Mangrove and salt marsh now weight each cell by the share of it the habitat covers, rather than crediting a whole cell to any extent that clips it. Mangrove extent falls 29.08 Mha to 14.60, which is the polygons' own area, and the EEZ-only total moves $22.84bn to $17.72bn. ⚠ Yanxu has not been told. Seagrass is unchanged, because its density is a polygon attribute rather than a per-pixel value. ⚠⚠ Its overlap double-count is now measured: the 293,147 WCMC polygons sum to 54.46 Mha but dissolve to 30.02, so overlaps inflate the extent 1.8 times, and the dissolved figure lands inside the 16 to 27 Mha range the author's own appendix cites from McKenzie. Not yet fixed, and worth raising with Yanxu rather than changing under him while he revises.
- **number:** Values the carbon held in mangroves, salt marshes and seagrass. Matches the author's reported numbers. EEZ-only gives $17.72bn while including the landward pixels gives $58.75bn, both after the coverage fix. It matched the author’s reported numbers before that fix, at $22.84bn and $102.18bn.
- **need:** Count only habitat pixels seaward of the shoreline, or the landward side too (4.5 times the total)? ⚠ **Settled with Yanxu Long, 2026-08-28.** He accepts the extent fix ("this makes sense to me, I'll double check"). Neither of the two rasters exists on his machine either, so the latitude step functions stay — and the appendix, `global_climate_regulation_coastal_carbon_appendix.docx`, documents them AS the method rather than as a fallback: salt marsh SOC is a four-bin latitude function based on Maxwell (36, 44, 50, 70 tC/ha), noting "a native raster from that source is not yet wired into the pipeline", and the mangrove BGB default is called out as overestimating "along dry-tropical coasts such as Arabia and northern Australia", which is the 42 percent of tropical mangrove measured here. ⚠ He is separately revising: reviewer comments, currency to 2019 international dollars, and disentangling zeros from missings. For their own paper he wants a newer base year and an annual time series with sea-level rise, so the GEP 2019 run and that paper will diverge.
- **signed off:** amber: examined, and at least one of the twelve conditions is not yet verified. ⚠ **10 is unmet here and everywhere**: no service in this library has been built from an empty project directory, so every claim that a clone reproduces it rests on the input paths resolving rather than on a run. ⚠ **11 is unverified**: the base year is 2019 across every service, but the country list, the true-zero-against-missing rule and the shared parameters have not been checked service by service

## Pollination

- **subgroup:** -
- **module:** pollination
- **category:** raster arithmetic
- **in the library:** yes
- **run:** yes
- **ours:** yes for the value raster, which the account's number comes from. We built production times the world producer price we build ourselves times each crop's dependence on animal pollination, over 153 crops. The sufficiency side weights that value by how much habitat sits near each field, and it belongs to the other caller rather than to this one: `configure_sufficiency` runs inside `pollination_shock`, which is a registered task with its own runner. A base-year account has no scenario for the weighting to vary against, so the GEP number is the value raster and the habitat weighting enters the scenario shock.
- **method:** Each crop's production raster times its world producer price times its pollination dependence ratio, summed over crops and priced at the GEP base year, then summed to countries. Coffee is blended by country from what it grows, because FAO files arabica and robusta under one item code with different dependence. The quantity is the CropGrids v1.08 production grid for 2020, a published gridded dataset.
- **total:** {{< meta poll_raster >}} without habitat sufficiency, {{< meta poll_with_sufficiency >}} with it, both at 2019 prices from our own raster.
- **code:** Folded in from the author's repo, then refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. The value raster is now built by a task in the tree: `pollination_value_raster` reads the 158 CropGrids production rasters from base data and writes USD in the cell. Two fixes: The raster carried USD per square kilometre while the code that summed it assumed USD per cell. The price and dependence lookups were built by collapsing a table on a duplicated key, so the value kept was whichever row came last. 
- **grid:** WGS84 geographic on the shared pyramid. Cell areas come from hazelbean on the WGS84 ellipsoid, adopted 2026-08-26 in place of a 6371 km sphere that differed by -0.22 to +0.56 percent with latitude. Correct now. ⚠ The earlier $18.28bn was this same raster summed with no cell area at all, so the grid is exactly where this service went wrong before.
- **reference:** No reference for the value, and two for the inputs, both pinned by tests as of 2026-09-01. Our `pollination_1993_2024.parquet` reproduces the author's published csv over all 287,285 rows, every one of its 22 numeric columns agreeing to 1.4e-14, the only difference being a missing label reading as None out of parquet and nan out of csv. And our rebuilt value raster sits 0.93 percent above his staged one, correlation 0.995 over 2,941,471 shared cells. ⚠ The entry previously said the source raster was reproduced to 1.8e-08. That number was measured once by hand and the comparison behind it stopped running when the library began building its own raster, so it is replaced here by the two figures a test recomputes. ⚠ We build the raster ourselves, so the second is two pipelines meeting rather than one reproducing the other; the first checks our port and not the science.
- **replicated:** The dependence panel exactly, to 1.4e-14 over 287,285 rows, and the raster to within 0.93 percent, both checked by a test on every run rather than measured once.
- **decided:** Cell areas moved to the WGS84 ellipsoid from hazelbean, the convention the rest of the account uses, costing 0.1086 percent. Country aggregation moved to the centre rule, costing 0.1211 percent of the world total and moving 92 of 204 countries by more than 5 percent.
- **number:** Values the crop output pollinators are responsible for. **$387.67bn at 2019 prices over 193 countries**, from the raster our own chain builds — FAO panel, yield-change ratios, Monfreda yields carried to the base year, CropGrids harvested area, our median price, the author's dependence table with coffee blended per country. ⚠⚠ **Changed on 2026-08-30 from $384.09bn**, which was the author's staged raster: the yield and production steps had no port until that day, so no run here could produce the value raster from source. Of the $3.40bn difference against his raster, **$2.98bn is the coffee blend** (FAO item 656 covers arabica at 0.25 and robusta at 0.65; his `load_poll_dep` keeps the first row, valuing every coffee country as pure arabica) and the rest is the per-cell versus density convention. Set `pollination_blend_coffee_dependence` to false and our pipeline returns his published pair exactly: **$384.97bn unweighted and $161.45bn weighted, both to the cent**, with the sufficiency raster identical to his in all 331,871,070 defined cells once the tile height is his 8192. Cell areas are WGS84 from hazelbean, the same convention the rest of the account uses through the ha_per_cell pyramid, which pollination alone did not: it was on a 6371 km sphere, differing by -0.223 to +0.557 percent with latitude, so the GEP total was summing services that measured a cell differently. Adopting it cost 0.1086 percent. Aggregated on the centre rule so a border cell goes to the country covering its centre rather than to whichever was rasterised last. That change cost 0.1211 percent of the world total and moved 92 of 204 countries by more than 5 percent, Iraq by 65.63. Vatican City, Gibraltar, Monaco and Macao drop out entirely, being smaller than a cell: $0.35M between them. From a raster we build (the original one was 2024). The previous $18.28bn was the same raster summed without cell area; area-weighted it gives $476.29bn. That figure is not an independent check: it comes from our own run of the source pipeline on 2026-07-25, which wrote both the raster and the summary beside it. What it does establish is that the source code treats the raster as a density, since its own summary area-weights what it wrote. The units are stated in that repo's methods_overview.md, 'global value raster (USD/km2)'. Fixing coffee's dependence adds $3.76bn at 2024 prices. Our code reproduces the author's raster to 1.8e-08. ⚠⚠ **Computed both ways on 2026-08-28**, one grid and one price year: production x price x dependence gives $388.47bn over the raster, and multiplying by 300 m habitat sufficiency built from `lulc_esa_2019` gives $163.46bn, a ratio of 0.421. The $388.47 against the published figure is the raster sum against the country zonal sum, which drops cells outside any country. William Sidemo Holm's 2019 equivalents are **$385bn and $190bn, ratio 0.494** (revised 2026-08-28 when he switched price and yield windows from mean to median; his 2026-08-27 figures were $387bn and $191bn, the same ratio). So we agree closely unweighted and discount harder weighted. He confirms `target_year` and `deflation_base_year` are both 2019 in his config, which we verified at lines 118 and 128. The gap is **not yet explained, and eight candidates are eliminated by measurement** (2026-08-28). Not the value raster's geography: his precomputed value raster under our sufficiency gives 0.4155, essentially ours. Not `fill_non_ag` — his runner calls `run_pollination_sufficiency_300m` without it, so both sides take the `None` default; this had been the prime suspect and is refuted. Not the constants: `_RADIUS_METERS` 2000.0, `_THRESHOLD` 0.30 and the `_AG_CLASSES`/`_NAT_CLASSES` sets are unchanged since his initial commit. Not the land-cover file: his `config/default.yaml` resolves `lulc_esa_{target_year}.tif` at `target_year: 2019`, the same map we read. Not the grids, all 0.05 degree 3600x7200 and 0.002778 degree 64800x129600. Not the aggregation: pixel-wise gives 0.4208 and an unweighted mean 0.7004, and his 0.4935 lies between them. Not the nodata convention: his valuation writes NaN as -9999, dropping cells we keep as zero, which moves ours only 0.4208 to 0.4291. Since his value raster under our sufficiency still gives 0.4155, **his sufficiency raster must differ from ours**. The target-year lead is also closed: commit `7f201c4` notes that before it "everything was set up for creating rasters with the target year 2020", but he states his current figures come from the new code with both years at 2019, and independently ESA 2019 and 2020 differ by only 0.0405 percent of pixels (agricultural cover +0.044 percent), far too little to move a ratio 7 points. **Twelve candidates eliminated, none remaining that we can test from outside.** Also refuted: the differences do NOT compound — every combination of value-raster choice, per-cell versus density units, and nodata denominator lands between 0.4155 and 0.4291, a spread of 0.014 against a gap of 0.064. Per-cell versus density weighting alone moves 0.4208 to 0.4169, and sufficiency barely correlates with latitude (-0.005), mean 0.577 in every band. `fill_non_ag` can only push the wrong way: filling non-arable with 0.0 and scaling by agricultural area fraction lowers sufficiency, and ours is already below his. Our 300 m raster was checked directly and is correct — 96.04 percent NaN for non-arable, 1.02 percent genuine zeros (arable with no habitat in range), 2.93 percent positive, so arable totals 3.95 percent, matching the ESA agricultural share exactly, and the 5 km average really is arable-only. Aggregation level does not explain it either: country value times unweighted country-mean sufficiency gives 0.6495, overshooting, while value-weighted gives 0.4203. His 0.4935 is bracketed by our numbers but reproduced by none of them. ⚠⚠ **Settled on 2026-08-28 by running HIS repository directly** (`scripts/pipelines/run_pollination_sufficiency.py --step sufficiency_300m` on `lulc_esa_2019.tif`, his config, our machine): his own code gives **$163.43bn, ratio 0.4207**, against our port's $163.46bn and 0.4208. ## Erosion Control

- **subgroup:** -
- **module:** erosion
- **category:** process model run here
- **in the library:** yes
- **run:** Yes, and the sediment step twice over. `intermediate/sdr_6p45km/` holds 1.1 GB of genuine InVEST SDR output from 2026-08-16 with a TaskGraph cache and the full set (usle, rkls, sed_export, sed_deposition, stream), all suffixed `2019_revised_dec_14`. The account does not read it: `erosion_sdr_results_suffix` is `2019_revised_feb_13`, which resolves to the author's rasters pulled from his drive in February. So the sediment model behind $18.24bn is his, with our own run sitting unused beside it. **Which vintage is current is settled and needs nobody asked:** his `feb_13` rasters are dated 19 February 2026 and his drive holds no other vintage, so February supersedes December and the account already reads the newest. Our own run carries the `dec_14` label only because `erosion_functions.py:405` hardcodes `"results_suffix": "2019_revised_dec_14"` as a default left over from the port; the name says nothing about the data's age, and it should be retired so a run cannot label itself with a vintage that no longer means anything. The `invest_sdr` task directory being 0 bytes is not evidence either way, because the outputs are configured into `sdr_6p45km` rather than into the task directory.
- **ours:** The valuation yes; the biophysics no. ⚠⚠ **Found by the first cold start, 2026-09-01: the `invest_sdr` task cannot run.** `run_invest_sdr(paths)` references `p` at line 113 and `p` is neither a parameter nor a module global, so it raises `NameError` on the first call. Thirteen other functions in `erosion_tasks.py` have the same shape. It has never been noticed because the task carries `skip if dir exists: 1` and the directory always existed, so a warm run skips it and a cold start is the only thing that executes it. There is no `intermediate/invest_sdr/` output in the warm project either, which is the corroboration. So the USLE and avoided-erosion rasters the account values are the author's staged files, `usle_2019_revised_feb_13.tif` and `avoided_erosion_2019_revised_feb_13.tif`, and our SDR step is decorative. What is ours is everything downstream of them: the prevention shares, the severity threshold, the elasticity join, the valuation and the country collapse.
- **method:** How it works, in six steps. **1.** InVEST SDR gives, for every pixel, how much soil erodes and how much stays. Which SDR rasters the account actually reads is a question about this run rather than about the method, and it is under **run**. **2.** A threshold picks out what counts as severe erosion, 11 tonnes per hectare per year or 2 for small and low-lying countries. That is SES-11, the author's baseline, and it is what our run is configured for: THRESH_HIGH 11.0 and THRESH_LOW 2.0, with nothing overriding them. The manuscript's EPS-5 relaxes the threshold to 5 as a sensitivity analysis rather than an alternative baseline, letting more land in and taking the reported figure from $14.59bn to $29.1bn. **3.** For each severe pixel, what share of the soil loss was stopped by the field's own vegetation (on-farm), and what share by vegetation upslope catching water before it arrives (upstream). **4.** The two are combined without counting twice: a field can be protected by both at once, so rather than adding them it asks, per pixel, the chance at least one of them saved it. On-farm protects 10.0 percent of production on average and upstream 10.8, and the combined share is 12.5 rather than 20.8, so the 8.4 point gap is production both mechanisms protect. **5.** Losing soil dents a harvest rather than destroying it, so a per-crop yield elasticity turns soil saved into output saved. It is small: median 0.153, range 0.080 to 0.259, so of the 12.5 percent of production on protected land only about 15 percent of that is output genuinely at stake. **6.** That output is priced at the FAOSTAT gross production value in constant 2019 USD, what the country's crops are worth. GEP = shock share times gross production value, an identity holding to 8e-13 across 177 countries, which is a largest absolute disagreement of 4.5 hundred-thousandths of a dollar. ⚠ Two things look like errors and are not. The union in step 4 is per pixel while a country's share is an average over pixels, so at country level combined is not 1-(1-onfarm)(1-upstream); averaging breaks the formula, which is arithmetic rather than a bug. Money is summed rather than averaged, so the dollars do reconcile exactly: on-farm $10.298bn plus the incremental upstream $3.661bn gives the combined $13.958bn. The formula in one line: soil loss prevented on cropland, on-farm and upslope combined as a union rather than a sum, turned into a crop production shock weighted by each crop's production and its yield elasticity to erosion, times the country's crop gross production value.
- **total:** $18.24bn
- **code:** Folded in from the author's repo, then refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. The prevention shares, the severity threshold and the valuation are in the science module, tested. Added the step that builds the upstream prevention share by routing the erosion rasters down the DEM, because the author's code expects `upstream_prevention_share.tif` to already exist from a workflow outside his repo, so the pipeline could not run off his cluster. The formula is his, followed from `author_drive/code_v2/upstream_PS_20260302.ipynb` — accumulated avoided erosion over accumulated RKLS, a ratio, so the pixel area cancels — but the D8 routing comes from pygeoprocessing rather than the notebook's own implementation. Checked against his own output as of 2026-08-27: his `upstream_prevention_share.tif` was fetched from MSI and sits at `author_drive/msi_upstream_attribution_v3/`, on the same grid, and ours reproduces it — mean 0.77983 against his 0.77945, a ratio of 1.0005, median difference zero, and 87.5 percent of the 7,030,834 valid cells within 0.01. The four upslope attribution layers came with it, so the diagnostics his code reads are no longer missing and the parameters now point at his files. The build step stays, because it is what lets the account run on a machine that cannot reach his cluster. Three fixes. The severity threshold is lower for small countries, and because r264 splits six countries into territories, a single territory’s area could make a country look small; areas are now summed per country. Measured on that file, the countries whose small/large status can turn on it are CHN, FRA, GBR, IND and TUR. The 40 paths that pointed at two specific machines now come from es_parameters, and a missing row raises an error naming it rather than falling back to a directory that does not exist. And the SPAM reprojection uses hazelbean rather than rioxarray, byte-identical and about 11 times faster per band. Added the `gep_calculation` the service had never had: it wrote its country totals into integrated_country_gep.csv, which is wide and carries the on-farm, upstream and combined components side by side, so nothing downstream could read it. It now writes the same per-country table as every other service, on the combined component.
- **grid:** Equal Earth (EPSG:8857), an equal-area projection, so `pixel_area_hectares` computes one constant from the resolution and that is exact. It raises on an unprojected CRS rather than assuming, which is the pattern worth copying. Correct.
- **reference:** The author's methodology and July manuscript, both staged at `base_data/global_invest/erosion/author_drive/results/`. They report **$14.59bn across 164 countries** under the baseline severe-erosion scenario SES-11, against our $18.24bn, positive in 161 countries, so ours sits 25 percent above his. ⚠⚠ The country split does not agree: against the six largest reported, ours puts China 30 percent higher ($3.87B against $2.97B), India 28 percent lower ($0.79B against $1.10B) and the Philippines 41 percent higher ($0.72B against $0.51B), and the ranking reorders. Offsetting country errors are exactly what a matching total hides. ⚠ Those figures come from a run that predates the country-area fix under **decided**, so they are not what the current code produces; the rerun that will restate them is still going.
- **replicated:** Yes, against his corrected run, to 0.8%. His `outputs_corrected_20260829` gives $18.0940bn over 162 positive countries and 193 mapped; ours gives $18.2409bn, 161 and 192. ⚠ The entry said 25% against his March table until 2026-09-01; that comparison was superseded by his corrected run and by the elasticity crop-name fix he found, and quoting it now would be wrong. The residual is the border rule and nothing else: his notebook sets `RASTERIZE_ALL_TOUCHED = True`, ours assigns a cell to the country whose polygon covers its centre, which puts 1.005% more cells inside a country on the real analysis grid. Everything upstream is identical -- crop GPV to the cent across 201 countries, threshold policy for all 250, and the USLE, avoided-erosion, price and elasticity files byte-identical by sha256. ⚠ The 0.8% is not spread evenly: 71 of 162 countries agree within 1% and 25 differ by more than 5%, the archipelagos, deltas and mountain borders where the two rules disagree most. The global total is robust to the choice; some country figures are not.
- **decided:** Three changes made rather than asked about, and one observation to pass on. **Country attribution:** a border cell goes to the country covering its centre. Under all-touched, which his code sets and ours did too, every country whose outline touches a cell claims it and the one rasterised last keeps it, so a country's value moved with its row order in the boundary file. **Boundary file:** `ee_r250` rather than `ee_r264_correspondence`. It changes no number here, measured: r264's 264 features carry the same 250 countries, total area is identical to six decimals, and `rasterize_iso3` already assigned one id per ISO3, so the six China rows always shared one and were never summed twice. What it removes is a class of error rather than an instance. The severity threshold reads a *country's area*, and on r264 a country arrives as several rows, which is exactly how a single territory's area could make a large country look small and draw the low soil-loss tolerance. On r250 that cannot arise, because nothing is split. It also puts erosion on the same file every other aggregation uses, which is the standing rule (r250 for sums, r264 for maps). **Country area:** a country's area is the sum of the territories the boundary file splits it into. That matters on r264, where China and India each arrive as six rows and a single territory's area let them qualify as *small* and draw the low soil-loss tolerance, enlarging the domain the threshold defines; the countries whose status can turn on it are CHN, FRA, GBR, IND and TUR. On r250 it cannot arise, because nothing is split there. **South Sudan:** it was dropping out of the FAO join and taking a zero, against the author's $3.71M, and the cause was ours. `ee_r264_correspondence` carries the country as `SSD` under `iso3_r250_label` and as `SDS` under the Natural Earth columns `adm0_a3`, `sov_a3` and `su_a3`; the boundary loader preferred `adm0_a3`, so the run keyed on a code the FAO tables do not use and its crop GPV came back empty while the physical side computed normally. Fixed twice over: `ee_r250` carries no `adm0_a3` at all, so the boundary move settles it on its own — the live rerun already shows `SSD` on the default high threshold — and the loader now prefers `iso3_r250_label`, which is the canonical label, so no other file carrying Natural Earth columns can shadow it. flood had already met this and remapped SDS to SSD; erosion had not.
- **number:** Values the crop production that soil retention protects: the share of soil loss prevented by a field's own cover and by everything upslope of it, turned into a production shock and priced against the country's crop output. $18.24bn across the 192 countries that carry a value, of which 31 compute an exact zero, leaving 161 positive. The author reports $14.59bn across 164 countries for the same SES-11 baseline, so ours sits 25 percent above his, and the country split diverges further still. South Sudan is dropped because the source table spells it SDS where the country table uses the ISO SSD; its value is zero, so no dollars are lost by it today.

## Landslides

- **subgroup:** -
- **module:** landslide_mitigation
- **category:** process model run here
- **in the library:** yes
- **run:** yes
- **ours:** yes
- **method:** Slope stability computed with and without forest root cohesion, into landslide hazard and expected deaths, times a GDP-adjusted value of a statistical life. The quantity comes from a slope-stability model run here, twice per pixel.
- **total:** $770.7M (570.66 avoided deaths, not in any committed table)
- **code:** Folded in from the v0.2.0 release, then refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Added the `gep_calculation` the service had never had: it wrote country totals into a zonal-statistics file that nothing downstream read, so the service had a run and no report. It now writes the same per-country table as every other service, summing the sub-region rows per country because the zonal table is on r264. Two small fixes: the option meant to force a step to rerun actually disabled it, and the figure step ignored the setting that says whether to run at all.
- **grid:** EASE-Grid (EPSG:6933) at 1 km, an equal-area projection, so `pixel_area_m2 = pixel_size_m ** 2` read off the reference raster is exact. It needs a projected grid rather than merely tolerating one: flow accumulation counts upslope pixels and that count only becomes an area if every pixel covers the same ground. Correct, on the same grounds as erosion.
- **reference:** None machine-readable. A per-country output from a v0.2.0 run has been asked for and not received, so $770.7M and 570.66 avoided deaths rest on our run alone.
- **replicated:** Nothing to match: no machine-readable reference has been received.
- **decided:** -
- **number:** Values the deaths that forest root cohesion prevents. Computed end to end, the full run gives 570.66 avoided deaths, $770.7M. No reference output exists to check it against. 
- **need:** One per-country output from a v0.2.0 run, and its input versions. This is also the one service that builds its own value of a statistical life, from the OECD country table deflated from 2022 to 2019 USD with an income-group fallback, so it is the row that has to move onto the air quality group's shared table for the account to price a death the same way everywhere. That move will change the number, because the two sources differ. The same three questions apply to that table as on the air filtration row: its currency year, an ISO3 column rather than a country name, and the countries it does not cover, which is what the income-group fallback is for.

## Crop Production

- **subgroup:** commercial
- **module:** crop_provision
- **category:** table arithmetic

- **run:** yes
- **ours:** yes, on the same footing as energy production rather than mining. FAOSTAT publishes the market value of the crop, not the part of it that belongs to nature, so no published figure is being relabelled. What is adopted is the CWoN land rental rate, and it is the entire attribution.

The quantity comes from a CSV, FAOSTAT gross production value.

## Crop Production

- **subgroup:** subsistence
- **module:** crop_provision
- **category:** table arithmetic
- **in the library:** yes
- **run:** yes
- **ours:** yes
- **method:** Cropland area times the regional share of agricultural area in farms under two hectares (Lowder et al. 2021) times FAOSTAT's value of agricultural production per hectare times the share of crop production value a household consumes rather than sells (FAO RuLIS national surveys), attributed by the CWoN land rental rate and deflated to the base year by each country's own CPI. A surveyed country's missing years are filled from a per-country regression on year, GDP per capita and commercial production; an unsurveyed country is filled from a global regression on cropland area.
- **total:** $23.78bn
- **code:** The reference pipeline ported stage for stage, so the library computes the figure rather than quoting it, and then departs from it in three places, each deliberate and each reported separately. FAOSTAT reports cropland in thousands of hectares against an intensity per single hectare and the Lowder share is a percentage, so each is read as its source labels it. Countries no survey reached take an imputed own-consumption **share** rather than an own-consumption **level** predicted from cropland area, so three of the four factors behind such a country are still its own. And the delivered table is put on the account's country list by the house collapse. The reference's own arithmetic runs through the identical stages in the same task and is published beside ours, which is what lets a reader check the port instead of taking it on trust.
- **grid:** No raster. The component works on country tables (it reads only CSV), so nothing multiplies a density by a cell area and the cell-area question does not arise. Verified 2026-09-01 by checking every read in the task.
- **reference:** The reference panel, reproduced. Running its arithmetic through our port gives $1,832,260,428.28 against its published $1,832,260,428.28 across 66 countries, largest per-country relative difference 2.3e-14. Each stage was checked separately on the way: 73 own-consumption rows to 1.3e-16, 63 interpolated rows to 1.9e-16, and the extrapolation choosing the same covariate and the same 49 observed / 1,339 predicted / 222 missing split. ⚠ Same lineage, so it tests the port and cannot see an error the reference's code also makes; where we found one, we publish our own arithmetic rather than theirs.
- **replicated:** Yes, exactly, and the reproduction is published as its own column rather than asserted. ⚠ Same lineage, so it tests our port rather than the science.
- **decided:** The account's figure is ours, not the reproduction, and on three counts. The units: FAOSTAT's cropland is in thousands of hectares against an intensity per single hectare and the Lowder share is a percentage, so reading each as labelled is the method done correctly rather than a variant of it. And the imputation: what the survey measures is a share, a ratio of two quantities that move together and travel between countries, where the reference predicts the level from cropland area -- which is the largest term in the formula that produced the level it is fitted to, so the fit is close to circular and the fitted rows outnumber the observed ones twenty-seven to one. Publishing either as the account's number once we knew would have been repeating a mistake with our name on it. And the currency: the account reports 2019 US dollars and reads FAOSTAT current-year values as already being that, which holds for the Value of Production table but not for the production intensity, which FAOSTAT publishes only in international dollars. There is no current-US$ version of that element to read instead, so the estimate is converted -- by the factor FAOSTAT's own two publications of the same agricultural output imply, not an external table. It moves the figure 4.6%, from $24,930,567,445 to $23,780,485,591, and 48 of the 66 countries carry their own factor with the rest on a regional median.
- **number:** **$23,780,485,591 across 66 countries, in 2019 US dollars**, and 72.3% of it rests on a country's own observed survey rather than an imputed share. Two further figures are published beside it so each departure from the reference is separable: $18,322,604,283 is the reference's own extrapolation with only the units corrected, and $1,832,260,428 is its arithmetic entirely, which reproduces its published panel. ⚠ The share imputation is not what drives the total: requiring anything from one to five surveys before a regional median is used, or forcing every unsurveyed country onto the global median, moves it only about 2%.
- **need:** Three findings to put to the authors, none of which our figure now depends on: the factor of ten above; the delivered file, which joins the panel against the correspondence on a Natural Earth name column and carries 16 of its own 66 valued countries at $398,356,097; and eleven countries whose observed survey values leave the panel at the interpolation step, Ethiopia among them, because a row missing GDP per capita or commercial production is dropped and its observation goes with it. Separately, and for the account rather than the authors: whether subsistence is added to commercial at all, given RuLIS reports own consumption as a share of crop production value that FAOSTAT's production figures already include.


- **signed off:** amber: twelve of the thirteen conditions hold as of 2026-09-01, and 9 does not. **1, 2 and 3 are met**: our code produces the figure, every step from the eleven staged inputs to the published number is a task in this library and it reads nothing from the reference repository, and the figure is from the current code. **4 is met**: no raster, so no cell area. **5 and 12 are met, and the check is real rather than nominal**: the port was verified stage by stage against the reference's own committed intermediates rather than only on the final total, their panel is staged in base_data, a test compares against it on every run present, and the agreement is claimed of the cold start. **6 and 8 are met**: the three gates pass and it adds no file to the service. **7 is met as of 2026-09-01**: it was open while the account's figure was the reference's arithmetic, because whether we published $1.83bn or $18.32bn changed the number; the account now publishes ours and the reference's beside it, so nothing outstanding moves the figure. Whether subsistence is added to commercial remains open but is for the account to decide and does not change what the code computes. ⚠ **9 is open**: the three findings have not been put to the authors, and the condition counts an unasked question as open. **10 is met**: `projects/gep_crop_provision_coldstart_20260901_122846`, run 2026-09-01, a fresh timestamped directory reusing nothing and seeded from `input_template/`, every input resolving inside the shared base_data. Reproducing the reference is claimed **of that run**, not of a warm one: the cold start returns $623,117,396,403 against the staged reference's $623,117,396,403 over 176 countries to 3.4e-16, its subsistence reference column returns $1,832,260,428.28 against their published panel's $1,832,260,428.28 over 66 countries to 2.3e-14, and the account's own subsistence figure is $23,780,485,591. The two tests that check this scan every crop_provision run on the machine rather than one named directory, so a stale warm run cannot stand in for a fresh one -- which is how they caught two superseded cold starts from earlier the same day, both since removed. **11 is met**: 250 rows on the account's list, the 184 countries no estimate reached recorded as NA rather than absent. **13 is met**: nothing in the pipeline or its verification reaches into anyone's checkout. Every input and every reference output is staged in base_data, no path in `es_parameters` leaves it, and H22 checks that mechanically. The author's repository could be deleted tomorrow and this would still run, still produce the figure and still verify itself. ⚠ The second half of 13 is why the published figure is not the reproduction: our code departs from theirs on the units and on the imputation, and the entry says why in **decided**.
## Livestock Production

- **subgroup:** commercial
- **module:** livestock_provision
- **category:** table arithmetic
- **in the library:** yes
- **run:** yes
- **ours:** yes, and more so on one of the two value columns than the other. The service writes two, because two attributions of the same FAOSTAT gross production are on the table and the account has not chosen between them. `livestock_provision_gep` applies the CWoN land rental rate and gives $519bn; `livestock_provision_gep_feed_share` applies the share of animal intake that ecosystems grew and gives $1.37T. Neither FAOSTAT figure is a published ecosystem value, so nothing is relabelled. The rental-rate column adopts CWoN's attribution whole, while the feed-share column derives its own, computing each country's intake share from the GLEAM 3 dashboard rather than taking a published share.
- **method:** FAOSTAT gross production value (element 57, current USD) over 65 livestock products, times an attribution factor: either the CWoN land rental rate or the GLEAM share of feed intake that ecosystems provided. The quantity comes from a CSV, FAOSTAT gross production value over 65 products.
- **total:** $246bn on the rental rate. $653bn on the feed share. ⚠ It was $519bn until 2026-09-01, when the same group-total double count found in crop production was found here: the FAO item list carried "Livestock", the total FAOSTAT computes by adding every animal product, alongside those products themselves. It put 106 of 152 countries above 100% of their own livestock output, median 1.397. Keeping the group total only where no individual product is published leaves a median of 0.985 and 15 countries above, none by more than 45%, and those carry items FAOSTAT files outside "Livestock" -- beeswax, honey, silk cocoons. The feed-share attribution is written too and moves with it, by the same proportion.
- **code:** Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Plus a units fix. The feed share is now wired through the task layer, so a run writes the feed-share value beside the rental-rate one. Its method page was a copy of the crop provision text, describing crop items throughout; it has been rewritten for this service.
- **grid:** No raster. The service works on country tables (it reads only CSV and Excel), so nothing multiplies a density by a cell area and the cell-area question does not arise. Verified 2026-08-26 by checking every read in the module.
- **reference:** No reference output exists to obtain: `Urgendalai/gep_livestock_provision` commits two scripts with hardcoded `D:/Netcapteems/` paths and no data. What it does commit is the feed-share formula, and that reproduces exactly -- our `feed_share` against `lambda.py` recomputed from the same staged GLEAM table, 171 countries, largest difference 1.1e-16, pinned by a test. ⚠ Nothing checks the valuation half. ⚠ And the reference script reads FAOSTAT element **152**, gross production value in constant 2014-2016 international dollars, where this service reads element **57**, current US dollars. That is a different measure in a different currency, so the two would not agree even if an output existed.
- **replicated:** The feed-share factor, exactly, and pinned. The valuation has nothing to match, because the reference commits no output.
- **decided:** -
- **number:** Values livestock output and attributes the part of it nature provided. The 65-product FAO list gives $2.29T of gross production; the two attribution factors give very different answers from it: the CWoN land rental rate gives $519bn over 178 countries, the GLEAM feed share gives $1.37T over 171, a factor of 2.6. Provisional until that choice is made. The feed share comes from GLEAM 3 intake harvested from FAO's public dashboard for 231 countries, 205 matching a country in the account, giving a real share rather than a bound (median 0.73; Mongolia 0.998, India 0.911, Brazil 0.847, France 0.651, United States 0.567, China 0.513).
- **need:** Which factor the account attributes livestock value with. The code computes both, and they differ by 2.6 times, $519bn on the CWoN land rental rate against $1.37T on the GLEAM feed share. The rental rate is the crop method's factor. Also the compiled GLEAM extract (gleam3_dmi.xlsx) to validate our harvest against, the confirmation of which FAO products count as livestock, and one per-country output. And how the CWoN land rental rate was derived. It is the whole of the attribution and moves the total proportionally. ⚠ **Which attribution is the GEP table using?** It registers $1.488T, and no configuration we can run produces it: not either item list, either FAOSTAT vintage, with or without the group total, on either attribution. The nearest we have ever produced is $1,374,349,438,511, our own feed-share figure before 2026-09-01, which is 7.7% below it and rested on the double-counted gross, so reproducing it would not have been good news. But $1.488T is a feed-share-scale number rather than a rental-rate one, which suggests the table and this entry are reporting different attributions. That has to be settled before either figure is quoted.

## Recreation

- **subgroup:** -
- **module:** recreation
- **category:** process model run here
- **in the library:** yes
- **run:** yes

- **method:** Every 1 km cell scored as a recreation site, visits generated into the best sites by a gravity model from resident population and allocated UNWTO overnights, priced at the fuel cost of the trip. The quantity comes from a gravity model run here, generating visits into scored sites.
- **total:** $1.73bn provisional (a units question is open)

- **grid:** ⚠⚠ WRONG, and already flagged in the source rather than found here. The grid is EPSG:4326 and the travel-cost step is metric: `ring_distance = buffer_zone * pixel_size` with `pixel_size` read off the raster, so in DEGREES, multiplied by a fuel cost in USD per KILOMETRE. A degree is 111 km at the equator and 56 km at 60 degrees, so the distance is neither in km nor constant. This is the failure that decides which grid a service needs: an operation defined in metric units cannot run on a geographic grid. The port is faithful to the source, which is why it was left in place. It makes $1.73bn provisional.
- **reference:** None reachable. The author's output table is not available, so there is nothing to check the $1.73bn against and nothing that would have caught the units problem. ⚠ The only thing checked against a reference is the UNWTO workbook reader, which returns the same 3,610 rows. That tests the read and not the valuation.
- **replicated:** Nothing to match: the author's output table is not available.
- **decided:** -
- **number:** Values the recreation trips people take into natural sites, at the fuel cost of getting there. $1.73bn, provisional because the units question below would change it. Separately, the author's output table is not reachable, so there is nothing to check it against.
- **need:** One per-country results CSV from the author's own run, to verify the port by replication. And whether the travel-cost step intended kilometres. The code multiplies a fuel cost per kilometre by a distance measured in the raster's pixel units, which understates the value.

## Wildfires

- **subgroup:** -
- **module:** fire_protection
- **category:** table arithmetic
- **in the library:** yes
- **run:** yes
- **ours:** the valuation yes, the coefficients no. The district-year panel is staged, 494 MB over 2010 to 2023, and the run reads it rather than any committed output: avoided burned area, damage per acre and the three GEP variants are all computed here. What is not ours is the regressions those coefficients come from, which are read from the source repo's committed results. The panel carries burned area split by human and natural cause and the human-modification index the third regression splits on, so refitting is work nobody has done rather than data we lack.
- **method:** Burned acres avoided because fires persist less where nature dominates, from a per-country regression of burned area on last year's, times a per-acre damage value. The quantity comes from a CSV, the district-year burned-area panel, with the coefficients from their fitted regression.
- **total:** three variants: -$22.4bn / -$1.3bn / +$16.7bn
- **code:** Translated from R to Python, then refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Fixed: Kosovo (GADM XKO vs the account's XKX) and India's Z01 and Z07 fell out of the country join, leaving $34.09M attached to no country while still inside the total.
- **grid:** No raster. The service works on country tables (it reads only CSV and Excel), so nothing multiplies a density by a cell area and the cell-area question does not arise. Verified 2026-08-26 by checking every read in the module.
- **reference:** The source repo's output for all 161 units, from their committed regression coefficients. ⚠ Same coefficients, so it tests the port.
- **replicated:** Yes, all 161 units, from their committed regression coefficients. ⚠ Same coefficients, so it tests the port.
- **decided:** -
- **number:** Values the burned acres that nature prevents. Computes avoided acres and their valuation from their committed regression coefficients, and reproduces the source repo's output for all 161 units. Three regressions give three totals because they ask three different questions. Baseline persistence regresses a country's burned area on last year's, which says nothing about nature at all: -$22.4bn. The cause difference compares how strongly nature-caused fires persist against human-caused ones: -$1.3bn. The area difference compares persistence where nature dominates against where people do: +$16.7bn. Two of the three come out negative, meaning nature makes fire damage worse rather than better.
- **need:** Which of the three is the account's. Baseline persistence should not be: it does not isolate nature's role, so it cannot answer what nature protects. Between the other two, the area difference matches how the service is described, fires persisting less where nature dominates, and is the only one that comes out positive. That is an argument, not a decision, and it is not ours to make. Also: 89 of the account's 250 countries carry no value, and whether they are unvalued or dropped somewhere in the join has not been checked.

We hold the fitted prices but not the data they were fitted to, which is the one thing stopping us implementing the method note ourselves. - **category:** table arithmetic
- **in the library:** yes

The workbook gives us the deaths and the answer, and we multiply the deaths by a value of a statistical life read from its own source, then check we recover the workbook's answer. That value is ours to the extent the source allows: the valuation reads the air quality group's country table directly and sources 218 of the 250 countries from it, with only Macao and Palestine left on the workbook's own figure. So the workbook can be reduced to a deaths table, and eventually replaced.

- **code:** Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. The valuation multiplies the workbook's deaths by the value of life read from the air quality group's country table. Tests cover this channel and the dust one the sandstorm row reports, the fill rule for a country with no value-of-life figure of its own (it takes the mean of the countries that have one), the check that refuses the join when the workbook stops lining up with the country list, and that the value of life resolves each country to its own row, which matters because the workbook labels both Serbia and Kosovo "Serbia" and a join on the name would give Kosovo Serbia's figure. The workbook carries no country code, only row order, so it can be joined only by position, and a silent reordering would give every country its neighbour's deaths.

- **decided:** -
- **number:** Values the deaths vegetation prevents by taking pollution out of the air, $17.81bn, and reproduces the committed totals. The avoided-death counts are the deposition channel of the drive's workbook: deaths avoided because vegetation captures dry pollutant out of the air. They come from three models run in sequence: process-based emissions, then InMAP, then health impact functions. None is set up here, though InMAP itself is open source. We do not rebuild it and take its counts as given.
- **need:** Four things. **Serbia and Kosovo are swapped in the workbook**, which labels both rows Serbia: the row that is Serbia carries Kosovo's value of life, 2,288,310, and the row that is Kosovo carries Serbia's, 2,184,433. We read them the right way round from the table, so the account is correct and the workbook is not. Macao and Palestine are priced per country in the workbook, at 10,396,302 and 1,662,995, but appear nowhere in the table, so those two values have no source we hold. Which currency year the table is in, since our accounts are 2019 constant USD and a different base would rescale every mortality total. And an ISO3 column, because the table keys on a slugged country name and thirteen countries need a hand-written alias to match. Separately, what emissions inventory and meteorology a global InMAP run needs, which is what would let us produce the deaths rather than read them.

- **code:** Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. The country totals are now computed from the drive's value raster rather than read from its summary table, and tested against the committed output.
- **grid:** EPSG:4326 geographic at 10 arc-second, summed flat with no cell-area weighting, and the file carries no units metadata. Measured 2026-08-26: the flat sum is $88.74bn over 265,210,379 cells and matches the committed output exactly, while area-weighting it would give $708.47bn, a ratio of 7.98 which is the value-weighted mean cell hectares. ⚠ The appendix documents the INPUTS as per hectare (yield in m3/ha, price per m3, a dimensionless GTAP land share), which makes a flat sum look wrong. The economics says otherwise: flat is about $42 per hectare per year of managed forest, which is an ordinary forest land rent, and the density reading is $337 and a global total larger than the whole forest-products industry's value added. So the raster is almost certainly already per cell and the code is right. What is undocumented is where the per-hectare chain became per-cell, and the appendix does not say.
- **reference:** The committed output for all 166 countries, reproduced exactly. ⚠ It cannot settle the units question above on its own, because it was produced by summing the same raster the same way. What settles it is the magnitude, independently: $42 per hectare is a forest land rent and $337 is not.
- **replicated:** Yes, exactly, for all 166 countries. ⚠ It cannot settle the units question, because we reproduce it by inheriting the same constant cell area.
- **decided:** -
- **number:** $88.74bn. Sums the value raster to countries and matches the committed output for all 166 countries, $88.74bn. What we cannot rebuild is the raster itself: making it needs a forest-management mask saying which forest is available for harvest, and that mask is not derivable from the layers we hold.
- **need:** The forest-management mask behind the value raster, or the code that builds it. And a decision on the factor share. Timber is the one service whose ecosystem share does not come from CWoN. Following Damania et al. (2023) it multiplies gross returns by the GTAP 10 land factor share for each of the 18 agro-ecological zones, so it does vary by zone rather than being one economy-wide number, but it is a different source and a different construction from the CWoN rental rate every other service uses. That matters because the account adds the services together, so the share attributable to nature should mean the same thing across them. ⚠ Switching is not a configuration change: no CWoN timber rent is staged anywhere in base_data. The CWoN files we hold cover crop, livestock, fisheries, renewable energy, extractive energy and non-wood forest products, and `ntfp/cwon_nwfp_value_per_ha.csv` is non-wood, a different quantity. CWoN 2024 does carry timber, as a land asset category beside agricultural land, forest recreation, non-wood forest products and forest water services, so the rent exists and the gap is that we do not hold the file. The two approaches are also closer than the source difference suggests: SNA and SEEA-CF count forest timber as an asset only where it can be logged commercially at a profit, which is the same restriction as the missing forest-management mask.

## Floods

- **subgroup:** -
- **module:** flood
- **category:** process model run here
- **in the library:** yes
- **run:** ⚠⚠ **Our refactored code ran the full valuation chain for the first time on 2026-08-29** (MSI job 17378863, 1h13m). It reproduces the source pipeline: ead $887.828bn, ead_nc $194.256bn, ead_ncplus $551.052bn, each to a ratio of 1.0000000, over 250 countries, with the largest single-country difference $6,098 on a $887.8bn total -- 7 parts in a billion, which is accumulation order rather than method. It also carries `ead_attributed_to_spa_usd2019` at $197.355bn, which the earlier runs omitted because Section C had not been run. Getting there took three fixes, all of them OUR refactor's requirements rather than his: run_flood.py still imported the deleted flood_paths module so the package could not be imported at all, the MSI runner had to supply flood_root_dir, and publish_inputs needed the shared country correspondence his code never reads. Before this, every 'our' flood run was actually his code.
- **ours:** the damage yes; the ecosystem share not fully. ⚠⚠ The counterfactual amplification rasters are an input we cannot produce: `_open_amp` reads them and, when they are absent, names `counterfactual/build_amplification_rasters.py` — a script that is not in this repository. The builder exists only in the author's copy on MSI, as `code/global_invest/flood/counterfactual/build_amplification_routed.py`. Until it is folded in, our GEP rests on 37 staged layers (about 100 GB) that our code can read and not rebuild, which is the same standing as erosion reading his USLE rasters. ⚠⚠ **The whole tree ran here on 2026-08-30 and 2026-08-31** (MSI jobs 17529966 and 17589055), so flood is no longer among the services we hold and have not run, where stormwater and air filtration still sit. The MSI setup that needed doing is done: the run writes to /projects/standard/jajohns/shared/gep_flood with its machine-specific inputs in that project's input/. ⚠ `gep_calculation` still reads his per-country export as an interim, so the account carries his $11.40bn rather than one we derived; 17589055 is the first run that could replace it.
- **method:** Flood depth by return period, through JRC depth-damage curves, times asset value per pixel, integrated into an expected annual damage. Five lettered sections, one task each. 

1. **A, inputs.** Download the JRC depth rasters (metres of standing water at each pixel for the 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 500-year floods) and warp them onto the LULC reference grid, so no later step re-warps. Build the LULC-to-SDA mapping. 
2. **B, SDA.** Delineate the service-demanding areas, the assets exposed to flooding. A pixel qualifies when standing water exceeds `flood_depth_threshold_m`, 0.1 m, AND its ESA class is one the mapping counts: 190 built-up, 10/11/12/20/30/40 cropland, 130 pasture. Each country is windowed out of the global grid, and `flood_all_touched` is false, so a border pixel belongs to the country covering its centre, the same centre rule erosion uses. This is the expensive section: the grid is 112,582 x 74,596, about 8.4 billion pixels, and every country is cut from it once per return period, so 250 x 6 = 1,500 passes write 3,000 rasters. 
3. **C, service flow.** Reproject the precomputed upstream SPA ratio onto each SDA grid and keep it where there is demand, `flow = where(sda_mask, spa_ratio, 0)`. ⚠ The service-providing area is NOT delineated here. From the author's appendix it is land whose cover retains rainfall that would otherwise run off, curve-number potential retention thresholded to a binary mask, and the ratio is the share of each demanding cell's upstream catchment that is service-providing. That is why the file we read is continuous between 0 and 1, mean 0.22, while the mask behind it is binary. Built per continent, mosaicked by `mosaic_counterfactual.py`. ⚠ The appendix is explicit that this supports no marginal statement: the SPA covers 48 to 77 percent of drained land by continent, and the threshold producing that is a statistical convention rather than a physical criterion. 
4. **D, valuation**, in four substeps. **4A** converts the canonical JRC EUR2010 table into USD2019 curves. **4B** computes damage per pixel per return period. There is no asset-value raster, and this is where the money enters: `jrc_max_damage_values_long_with_iso3.csv` gives a maximum damage in EUR per m2 for each country crossed with land type, what a square metre is worth when the water destroys it outright, and the JRC curves give a fraction between 0 and 1 per region, land type and depth. `damage_per_m2 = max_damage_eur_m2 * fraction`, so the per-pixel value is per-country, per-land-type EUR/m2 scaled by how deep the water is, never a mapped asset stock. Below 0.1 m a pixel is not flooded; the curves run to `flood_depthbin_max`, 6.0 m. **4C** integrates across return periods into an expected annual damage per country. **4D** consolidates the per-country files into the global table. 
5. **E, maps.** The figures. 

    The GEP is produced by none of these: it is `ead_bare - ead_current`, the difference between damage in a counterfactual degraded world and damage today, computed by `task_compute_flood_gep` in a separate tree. ⚠ The source scripts numbered the valuation section 4 with no steps 1 to 3, and its outputs used to carry `step4x` names; they are named for what they hold now, with the correspondence to his scripts in `flood/reference/output_provenance.csv`.
- **total:** $112.78bn
- **which number is which:** Five figures appear in this entry and they are five different quantities, so read this first. **$112.78bn** is ours: expected annual flood damage that occurs, recomputed here, and it is what the `total` row means. **$110.59bn** is the source pipeline's own summary of that same quantity, which is why reproducing it settles the port. **$887.828bn** is undefended expected annual damage, a larger quantity because it is before flood protection, and it is the figure the author publishes and the one our runs are checked against. **$11.40bn** is the GEP, the damage ecosystems prevent, `ead_bare - ead_current`, and it is the only one of the five the account carries; it is still his figure rather than one we derived. **$17.601bn** is tonight's superseded run, kept only because it is how the damage-table defect was found. ⚠ The first three are damage, the fourth is the service, and an entry that lists them without saying so invites someone to compare two of them.
- **code:** Refactored onto the library template and hazelbean conventions. Every step of the flood calculation was rewritten as a function.
- **grid:** Web Mercator (EPSG:3857) at 537.23 m, which is neither the shared pyramid nor equal-area. The damage pass used to give every cell one constant 288,615 m2, the equator value, while true ground area falls as cos squared of latitude to 14.43 ha at 45 degrees and 1.93 ha at 75; weighting by country latitude moves the total about -28 percent. **Fixed in code on 2026-08-26 (`6dadedf`)**: each row's latitude is transformed to WGS84 and the cell area computed from it, so a cell now carries its own ground area. ⚠ The outputs have NOT been regenerated, so every published flood number still carries the equator constant. The SDA layer is built from ESA-CCI, natively EPSG:4326 at 0.002777778, which IS the pyramid. ⚠ Corrected 2026-08-31: Section A does not reproject it out. `flood_lulc_path` reads `lulc_esa_2019_int_reproj.tif`, EPSG:3857 at 537.23 m, a copy reprojected before it was staged, and Section A warps the JRC depth rasters ONTO that grid. So the pyramid is left upstream of this repository, in one input, and everything downstream inherits it because the LULC file defines the reference grid.

Staged in base_data with his full 21-column account and both of our run's variants, and pinned by a test as of 2026-09-01. It agrees **to the cent, country by country**: 250 of 250 join, largest absolute per-country difference $0.000000, totals $11,403,596,548.37 against his $11,403,596,548.35. ⚠ One country differs and the test names it rather than hiding it in a tolerance: Iceland is NaN in his table and 2.1 cents in ours, which is the whole of the 162-against-163 positive-country count. ⚠⚠ Same lineage: the module is his pipeline with our path handling and ProjectFlow wiring, so this agreement was close to guaranteed. It is a build test -- it catches our refactor breaking his arithmetic and says nothing about whether the arithmetic is right.
- **replicated:** Yes, and now on the number that matters rather than only its input.
